claims.text: High configurational entropy induces large lattice distortions in near-equiatomic, single-phase nanoparticles.
Large lattice distortions slow atomic diffusion.
Slower atomic diffusion suppresses surface segregation and phase separation under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
The initial nanoparticles have a uniform chemical composition and significant lattice distortion.
Slight deviations from equiatomic composition reduce configurational entropy.
Slight deviations from equiatomic composition can promote formation of a multiphase structure.
A compositionally induced multiphase structure has lower lattice distortion than the equiatomic single-phase baseline.
Temperatures of 773–1173 K and 473–1923 K represent service conditions for catalytic and thermoelectric operation, respectively.
Severe lattice distortion hinders atomic rearrangement.
Sluggish diffusion minimizes both thermodynamic and kinetic drivers for phase separation and surface segregation.
Near-equiatomic, single-phase nanoparticles with high lattice distortion will retain phase and chemical uniformity after high-temperature exposure.
Compositionally modified multiphase nanoparticles will exhibit more phase separation or chemical segregation than the single-phase baseline under identical exposure.
Strictly equiatomic compositions naturally form single-phase structures.
Strictly equiatomic single-phase structures have high lattice distortion.
Surface-energy effects can dominate stability at extreme nanoparticle sizes.
Highly reactive environments or rapid sintering can alter diffusion behavior enough to invalidate the proposed mechanism.
The qualitative link between lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion is supported by prior evidence.
Statistically similar phase stability and chemical uniformity in the two nanoparticle sets would falsify the proposed differential effect of lattice distortion.
